content: docs#ZMod is semireducibly but not reducibly equal to either docs#Int or docs#Fin depending on its arguments. This is a big issue now that tactics respect transparency. What should we do? Do we make it implicit_reducible or do we turn it into an inductive type?
What is the issue here? Since tactics respect transparency, this is just a type of its own, with its own instances. Are there places where we abuse the defeqs?

As a user, it is very easy to get yourself in a pickle:

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic

example {q : ℕ} (r : ZMod (q + 1)) : r = 0 := by
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := r
  -- The LHS and RHS don't have reducibly the same type anymore

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Since tactics respect transparency

Rewriting tactics respect transparency. Other tactics (such as obtain and intro) do not.
As i have said time and time again, no type should be exactly semireducibly equal to another. They should either be implicit-reducibly equal or not equal at all
This is to ensure that all tactics see types the same way
Isn't the solution here to make ZMod more irreducible so one cannot use obtain?
For example here n and hn are super confusing for a mathematician.
Yeah sure, that's the inductive type approach I suggest above

Yaël Dillies said:

As i have said time and time again, no type should be exactly semireducibly equal to another. They should either be implicit-reducibly equal or not equal at all

I disagree very strongly with that: using defeqs carefully is an extremely powerful proof technique, and I don't think we should forbid it. But it should be used with care. In your example, obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := r is just bad: if you want to prove a statement on Fin n, just state it on Fin n. If you want to work with ZMod, just use its API -- unless you known exactly what you are doing, and why.

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic

example {q : ℕ} (r : ZMod (q + 1)) : r = 0 := by
  with_reducible obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := r

This fails. I wonder if this means we should make with_reducible obtain the default, and then have some kind of opt-in like with_unfolding obtain, or obtain!.
Having obtain and obtain!, and even the same for apply, refine, and so on, would be very reasonable imho.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Having obtain and obtain!, and even the same for apply, refine, and so on, would be very reasonable imho.

I suppose this will further distinguish it from using have in the same way , which could be a good thing (IIUC),

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

I disagree very strongly with that: using defeqs carefully is an extremely powerful proof technique, and I don't think we should forbid it

I wholly agree that we should not forbid all defeqs, but conversely there is no reason to allow all defeqs. Allowing too many defeqs is a major usability footgun for new and advanced contributors alike, and you should not expect anyone to remember what is a "good" defeq vs what is a "bad" defeq. My view is that the only defeqs that should exist are the good ones. For example, is there any reason not to forbid the ZMod (q + 1) = Fin (q + 1) defeq?

In other words, your sentence...
Sébastien Gouëzel said:

using defeqs carefully is an extremely powerful proof technique

... amounts to "If you don't like error messages, don't make errors!". I hope you can see how this is an untenable position from the point of view of learning Lean and mathlib

I don't understand what you're saying. If you're in a proof and take a wrong turn, then the result is not provable any more. Sure. That's unavoidable. So yes, if you want to get a working proof, don't make errors. The system should help you in this direction, but can't do everything. An advice like "don't unfold definitions, use the API" is good advice, but if someone tries not to listen, you can't do anything about it.

The problem is that it can be very hard to see whether and where defeq abuse is happening. I think @Yaël Dillies has a lot of first-hand experience of this from working on #38714.

If an expert finds it difficult to apply these rules, then what are we supposed to tell beginners? We should be striving towards a system where it is not possible to unknowingly make mistakes.

I would like to point out that there is this great new linter that tells you when you are making a mistake:

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic

set_option linter.tacticCheckInstances true

example {q : ℕ} (r : ZMod (q + 1)) : r = 0 := by
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := r -- warning
Are there any surprises that come from making ZMod instance reducible?

If we do that, then the instances on Fin (n + 1) apply to ZMod (n + 1) and vice versa, which would certainly not be ideal.

I'm not sure if this gives a noticeable slowdown in practice.
In particular, I believe we are trying to reduce our reliance on the CommRing (Fin n) instance
Ah, I forgot the instance was scoped for Fin but not for ZMod
